claims.text: An optimal laser fluence creates a balanced vaporization and rapid-quenching regime during pulsed laser ablation in liquid.
This balanced regime produces homogeneous, atomically mixed noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
Homogeneous, atomically mixed noble-metal HEA nanoparticles have enhanced catalytic performance.
The proposed starting material is a bulk noble-metal HEA target, such as Pt-Au-Pd-Ag-Ir, immersed in deoxygenated liquid.
An optimal-fluence condition is expected to yield more homogeneous nucleation than a higher-than-optimal fluence.
Pulse duration, repetition rate, and working distance will be held constant while fluence is varied.
Laser fluence controls the instantaneous temperature rise and subsequent quenching.
Temperature rise and rapid quenching mediate nanoparticle nucleation and alloy mixing.
At optimal fluence, the energy input is sufficient to vaporize or ablate the metal target and create a uniform plume.
Rapid plume cooling produces simultaneous nucleation and homogeneous alloy formation.
Excessive fluence causes overheating and nonuniform cooling.
Nonuniform cooling at excessive fluence causes phase segregation.
Phase segregation results in a heterogeneous distribution of catalytic sites.
Nanoparticles synthesized at optimal fluence will have a more single-phase, homogeneous alloy structure than particles synthesized at excessive fluence.
Nanoparticles synthesized at optimal fluence will show higher turnover frequencies or lower activation energies than particles synthesized at excessive fluence.
The hypothesis is limited to deoxygenated-liquid pulsed laser ablation with fixed pulse duration and repetition rate.
Changes in cavitation dynamics or environmental variables can alter nanoparticle formation.
The optimal fluence window may depend on real-time temperature and cavitation behavior.
Nonthermal effects may confound the relationship between fluence and nanoparticle formation.

The hypothesis is falsified if optimal fluence does not significantly improve both phase homogeneity and catalytic performance relative to the high-fluence baseline, or if fluence does not predominantly affect nucleation and quenching dynamics.
